summary:
Bolivia's 2016 Gender Identity Law grants legal recognition on the basis of self-declared identity through an administrative procedure, permitting a change of name and legal gender marker without surgery, sterilisation or a medical diagnosis. Gender identity is a protected ground in the country's anti-discrimination legislation.

The 2009 Constitution prohibits discrimination and protects bodily integrity: Article 15(II) addresses violence and Article 45(V) addresses maternity, while Title VIII of the Penal Code governs abortion. In January 2018 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights issued an advisory opinion on gender identity and same-sex family rights, and in December 2020 Bolivia's civil registry recognised free unions for same-sex couples.

Formal protection has not produced equal treatment in practice. The US State Department's 2011 Human Rights Report on Bolivia recorded the constitutional guarantee against discrimination alongside persistent societal discrimination against LGBT people, and a first national virtual survey published by Agencia Presentes in December 2024 found severe exclusion of LGBTI people across Bolivian society.
tangentialFactors:
Bolivia adopted the 2016 Gender Identity Law despite low voter support for trans rights. A study in Comparative Politics published in April 2024 found that trans activists secured direct access to legislators of the ruling party, and that statutes carrying contradictory heteronormative provisions were passed alongside it because both organised religion and LGBT activists functioned as party constituents. The outcome is a legal order that recognises trans identity while retaining family-law provisions framed around heterosexual norms.

Hostility inside state institutions is documented but thinly sourced. Reporting by eju.tv and La Razón of 25 August 2014 described homosexuality as taboo within Bolivia's armed forces, with gay soldiers giving anonymous testimony about discrimination and sanctions; the TLGB collective and human-rights campaigners were pressing for open service at that date. The inventory contains no equivalent material on trans personnel, so the treatment of trans service members cannot be established from these sources.
localsOnly:
Resident trans Bolivians correct name and gender marker through the administrative procedure created by the 2016 Gender Identity Law, which rests on self-declaration rather than clinical assessment. Constitutional anti-discrimination provisions and the protected status of gender identity in domestic legislation are the basis on which residents bring claims.

Same-sex couples have been able to register free unions since the civil registry recognised them in December 2020, following the Inter-American Court's January 2018 advisory opinion. Abortion continues to be regulated under Title VIII of the Penal Code, and the Constitution's Article 45(V) frames maternity as a protected condition, a provision resident advocates have criticised alongside other heteronormative statutory language.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved in this inventory: the day-to-day administration of the 2016 law at civil registry offices, including processing times, refusals and regional variation, and whether any documentary or notarial burdens persist in practice despite the statute's self-declaration basis.

Unresolved: enforcement of constitutional anti-discrimination provisions through the courts, the existence or absence of hate-crime sentencing enhancement for gender-identity-motivated violence, and any specialist protection or reporting machinery for trans people. No source here reports prosecutions or penalties relating to trans status.

Unresolved: entry and visa screening, airport document checks and the treatment of foreign visitors whose passports carry incongruent markers. Nothing in the inventory addresses whether a trans visitor's documents are accepted at Bolivia's borders, and the 2011 US State Department report predates the 2016 law by five years. Whether trans people may serve openly in the armed forces is also unsourced.
